title: Food and hosting
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: KOREAN HAS TWO NUMBER SYSTEMS, and L1-M8 used both in one module without ever saying which was which: han jan and du gae and se myeong are NATIVE numbers, ocheon won and samcheon won are SINO ones. The law, at last: native numbers COUNT THINGS and always take a counter; Sino numbers do money, minutes, dates and anything above ninety-nine. This rule explains something a learner already has, which is worth three rules that only add.

A COUNTER IS NOT OPTIONAL the way an English measure word is, and the order is fixed: NOUN, then number, then counter. maekju du byeong — beer, two bottles — which is the reverse of English's number-then-noun. Beside L1-M8's gae, myeong and jan this module adds byeong for bottles, geureut for bowls and inbun for portions.

THE HONORIFIC VERB SET ARRIVES AT THE TABLE, which is M1's decision made visible: meokda has a whole separate honorific word, deusida, so a host says deuseyo and masitge deuseyo and never meogeuseyo. This is the clearest of the four irregular honorifics — with gyesida (M2), jumusida and malsseumhasida (M1) — and a table is where a learner meets it first.

jal meogeosseumnida is said after eating and it is a FROZEN -mnida phrase, the third and last this course teaches, beside L1-M2's gamsahamnida and mannaseo bangapseumnida. It is not a licence to build -mnida forms: the speech level of this course is still -yo, and this phrase is learnt whole exactly as those two are.

Refusing without offence, and the cultural half is stated rather than judged. In Korean hosting THE OFFER IS REPEATED, and a bare aniyo is heard as politeness rather than as a decision — so the refusal that lands adds a reason: gwaenchanayo, bae bulleoyo. The other half a learner needs is the etiquette English has no equivalent for: the younger person pours for the older, and a glass is received with two hands.

words.note: Literally 'wheat wine'. It is counted in bottles or glasses and never on its own, which is what the counter is for.
The bottle counter, beside L1-M8's jan for glasses and gae for things. The number in front of it is native and shortens: han, du, se.

sentences.trap: The order is NOUN, number, counter — maekju du byeong — which is the reverse of English. And du and not dul, because a native number shortens in front of a counter exactly as L1-M8 showed with han jan.
sentences.sound: MAEK-ju du BYEONG joo-SE-yo. byeong is one syllable with the ng held.

mistake.why: Noun, number, counter — and the number shortens: Maekju du byeong juseyo.

sentences.usage: Ordering at any table where the food has already arrived.
sentences.mnemonic: Noun first. Then how many. Then what of.

words.note: bibim-, mixed, plus L1-M3's bap, rice. The name says what it is, which is true of a great deal of Korean food. inbun is its portion counter, and i-inbun — 'for two' — takes a SINO number.
A bowl, and the counter for anything served in one. It is also the ordinary word for the bowl itself.

sentences.trap: se and not set, the same shortening as han and du. The long forms hana, dul, set stand alone; the short ones go in front of a counter and nowhere else.
sentences.sound: bi-bim-BAP se GEU-reut joo-SE-yo. The final t of geureut is unreleased.

variations.changed: portions, which take a SINO number

mistake.why: The number shortens in front of a counter: se geureut.

sentences.usage: Ordering for a table, once everybody has decided.
sentences.mnemonic: hana, dul, set alone. han, du, se in front.

sentences.cue: The bibimbap is seven thousand won.

words.note: A SINO number, which is what money always takes — L1-M8's ocheon and samcheon are the same system. Native numbers never touch a price.

sentences.trap: Money is Sino and things are native, and there is no overlap. Ilgop, the native seven, cannot appear in front of won at all, which is the cleanest demonstration of the two-system law.
sentences.sound: bi-bim-BA-bi CHIL-cheon WO-ni-e-yo. chilcheon runs as two even syllables.

variations.cue: The beer is three thousand won.
The bibimbap, at least, is seven thousand won.
variations.changed: M3's topic particle and its contrast

mistake.why: Money takes Sino numbers: Bibimbap-i chilcheon won-ieyo.

sentences.usage: Reading a menu out loud, or checking a bill.
sentences.mnemonic: Native counts things. Sino counts money.

words.note: A whole separate honorific verb from meokda, not an ending added to it. A host says deuseyo; meogeuseyo does not exist.
L1-M9's masisseoyo turned into an adverb with -ge. Said to whoever is about to eat, and it is the closest Korean comes to bon appétit.

sentences.trap: There is no meogeuseyo. Four very common verbs have an ENTIRE honorific twin rather than the -si- infix — meokda becomes deusida, itda becomes gyesida, jada becomes jumusida, malhada becomes malsseumhasida — and the four are the four you meet first.
sentences.sound: ma-SIT-ge DEU-se-yo. The eu of deuseyo is the flat vowel, not an oo.

variations.changed: on its own, which is enough
the warmest of the three, and the commonest

mistake.why: meokda has its own honorific word: Masitge deuseyo.

sentences.usage: Said by the host as the food goes down, and answered by eating.
sentences.mnemonic: Four verbs have a twin, not an ending.

words.note: The offer word, and this module owns it. M9's comparative is built on this same deo, so it points back here rather than opening a row of its own.
Its opposite is jogeum, 'a little' — not M1's jom, which is the softener. The two are close in sound and do different jobs.

sentences.trap: deo is an offer and not a comparison. Nothing is being measured against anything here; the host is simply pressing more food on you, which is what a Korean host does.
sentences.sound: deo DEU-se-yo. deo is one short syllable, said with the mouth barely open.

variations.changed: the standing invitation rather than a second helping

mistake.why: The honorific of eating is deuseyo: Deo deuseyo.

sentences.usage: Pressed on you at least twice, and expected to be.
sentences.mnemonic: deo offers here. It compares in M9.

words.note: The belly. There is a second bae meaning pear, and this course teaches only this one — L1's homograph discipline, continued.
Said of the belly and never of a person: bae bulleoyo, the belly is full. gopayo is its opposite, bae gopayo, 'I'm hungry'.

sentences.trap: A bare aniyo will NOT end the offer. In Korean hosting the offer is repeated and a plain no is heard as politeness, so the refusal that lands is the one with a reason attached — which is what this sentence is.
sentences.sound: gwaen-CHA-na-yo, bae bul-LEO-yo. The ll is held.

variations.changed: the opposite, and the same shape
M1's thanks instead of the reason

mistake.why: A refusal needs a reason to land: Gwaenchanayo, bae bulleoyo.

sentences.usage: The third time more food is offered, and it will be offered a third time.
sentences.mnemonic: The belly is full, not you.

words.note: FROZEN, exactly like L1-M2's gamsahamnida and mannaseo bangapseumnida, and the third and last of them. It is not a licence to build -mnida forms; this course still speaks -yo.

sentences.trap: It is a whole phrase, learnt as one thing. Taking it apart to build other -mnida forms is the mistake the freeze exists to prevent, and this course teaches exactly three of them and no fourth.
sentences.sound: jal meo-GEO-sseum-ni-da. The final -da is light and often barely voiced.

variations.cue: Thank you for the meal. Thank you.

variations.changed: the -yo way to say much the same, and not frozen
a fuller English reading of the same Korean

mistake.why: The phrase is frozen and is said whole: Jal meogeosseumnida.

sentences.usage: Said on standing up from the table, to whoever fed you.
sentences.mnemonic: Three frozen phrases in the whole course. This is the third.

words.note: Meat in general. saengseon is fish and yachae is vegetables, and the three between them cover most of what anybody needs to say at a table.

sentences.trap: joahaeyo takes an OBJECT and joayo does not — L1-M9's distinction, and a menu is where it finally matters. gogi-ga joayo says the meat is good; gogi-reul joahaeyo says you like it.
sentences.sound: GO-gi-reul jo-a-HAE-yo. The h of joahaeyo is silent.

variations.changed: fish, which ends in a consonant so the particle is -eul
L1-M3's an, and the topic particle marking the contrast

mistake.why: joahaeyo takes an object: Gogi-reul joahaeyo.

sentences.usage: Answering what you would like, before the ordering starts.
sentences.mnemonic: joayo describes. joahaeyo takes an object.

words.note: An ordinary eating place rather than a smart one. The demonstrative joins it with a hyphen, because a bare i is the subject particle's key.

sentences.trap: masisseoyo is said of the PLACE as readily as of the food, which English does not do — a restaurant that is masisseoyo is one whose food is good, not one that tastes of anything.
sentences.sound: i-SIK-dang-i ma-SI-sseo-yo. The k of sikdang hardens the d after it.

variations.cue: This restaurant, at least, is cheap.
variations.changed: M3's cheap, with the topic particle
L1-M9's joayo, which is about the place rather than the food

mistake.why: masisseoyo is the whole predicate: I-sikdang-i masisseoyo.

sentences.usage: Recommending somewhere, or agreeing with a recommendation.
sentences.mnemonic: A place can be tasty in Korean.

sentences.cue: You take the drink with two hands.

words.note: With M4's -euro it means 'with', by hand: du son-euro, with two hands. Same particle, third job, and the family is now complete.
Receiving something handed to you, which is a different verb from taking it yourself. It is the verb the etiquette is built on.

sentences.trap: This is etiquette rather than grammar and English has no equivalent for it: the younger person pours for the older, and a glass is received with TWO HANDS. Doing it with one is not rude in a way anybody will mention, and it will be noticed.
sentences.sound: MAEK-ju-reul du SO-neu-ro BA-da-yo. son-euro runs as three syllables.
sentences.usage: At any table where somebody older is pouring.

comprehensionPool.cue: The bibimbap is seven thousand won.
You take it with two hands.
